subject: Default "print" in rstan, e.g. with summary

messages.author: 3ef7a01c7d912ca2
messages.subject: Default "print" in rstan, e.g. with summary
parts:
Whenever I do summary(..) in R, I expect some output to be printed by default when no assignment takes place. rstan is the only package I know of that behaves different, i.e. an explicit print(summary(mr.stan))  or (summary(mr.stan)) is needed.

When nothing comes out of summary(mr.stan), I intuitively do a sink() to counteract any suspected black hole. The same is true for other functions, such as extract, but it is most unexpected for summary.

Is there a reason for this? Did I miss something in the documentation? I personally believe that streamlining this to standard R behavior would be nice.

Dieter

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: Default "print" in rstan, e.g. with summary
parts:
On Tuesday, June 25, 2013 4:52:20 AM UTC-4, Dieter Menne wrote:
Whenever I do summary(..) in R, I expect some output to be printed by default when no assignment takes place. rstan is the only package I know of that behaves different, i.e. an explicit print(summary(mr.stan))  or (summary(mr.stan)) is needed.

When nothing comes out of summary(mr.stan), I intuitively do a sink() to counteract any suspected black hole. The same is true for other functions, such as extract, but it is most unexpected for summary.

Is there a reason for this? Did I miss something in the documentation? I personally believe that streamlining this to standard R behavior would be nice.

A lot of methods defined by rstan return things invisibly, meaning that the object is created if you assign to it and not otherwise. So,

s <- summary(fit)

creates an object called s whereas

summary(fit)

does all the same calculations but does not create an object.

Using invisible() so heavily is atypical for an R package, but Andrew never feels bound by R conventions. I think in this case, it is intended to discourage users from calling things like summary() unless they need the components of the list that summary produces. The canonical way to examine the output is to use the print() or show() methods on the fit object or just type

fit

which implicitly calls show() and then print(). Again, this is contrary to the rest of R where calling print() or show() would typically tell you some basic information about the model and summary() would give you coefficients, standard errors, etc. So, I would agree with you that this behavior is not great, but it is intentional.

Ben
